newsitem.title: CANADA: TENNIS-IVANISEVIC HOLDS ON FOR CANADIAN OPEN WIN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-IVANISEVIC HOLDS ON FOR CANADIAN OPEN WIN.

text.p: Second seed Goran Ivanisevic survived a roller coaster ride with New Zealander Brett Steven, prevailing in an exciting second round match that drew several standing ovations at the Canadian Open on Wednesday night.

The third-ranked Croat failed to convert five match points in the second set and fell behind 0-3 in the third before pulling out a 6-3 6-7 (8-10) 6-4 victory with the help of some timely aces and service winners.
"The crowd was unbelieveable and that helped me," said Ivanisevic.
Top seed Michael Chang had a much easier time as he moved into the third round when Australian Sandon Stolle retired with an upper arm injury with the American leading a 6-1 1-0.
"Maybe it would have been better to have a tougher match to start," said Chang, who had a first-round bye.
Third seed Thomas Muster shook off a slow start to demonstrate his new-found hardcourt prowess with a 4-6 7-6 6-3 victory over American qualifier Jeff Salzenstein
And fifth seed Thomas Enqvist of Sweden fought back to win a baseline battle with German Tommy Haas 6-7 6-4 6-4.
One seed fell Wednesday when Australia Patrick Rafter, seeded 11th, was upset by compatriot Michael Tebbutt, a qualifier ranked number 229th in the world.
But for the first time since the 1985 Canadian Open, all of the top eight seeds safely reached the round of 16.
Ivanisevic had several chances to end his contest much earlier. He squandered triple match point when he had the 68th-ranked Steven down 4-5, 0-40 in the second set.
Steven also fought off a pair of match points in the dramatic second-set tie-break.

Up 7-6 in the breaker, Ivanisevic appeared poised to win when Steven looked hopelessly off balance and out of position. But the New Zealander managed to win the sensational rally and drive the crowd to a frenzy when Ivanisevic finally hit a cross-court forehand passing shot wide.
Dropping the first three games of the third set only seemed to strengthen Ivanisevic's resolve.
"Maybe he thought I'm going down, but then I said, 'okay, let him finish if he can,'" recalled Ivanisevic.

"I broke him and then it was a very important game at 2-3. He had me love-40 and I hit three unbelieveable serves. After that I knew I was going to win the match," added Ivanisevic, who finishd with 23 aces and 12 service winners.

The fifth-ranked Muster, playing on hard court for the first time since he won the Lipton tournament in March, experienced some early difficulty with the 152-ranked Salzenstein's left-handed serve-and-volley game.
"I got down 0-2 in the second set but I broke right back and after that I felt better and better," Muster said.
After the second game of the third set, Salzenstein was treated for cramps.
"When he hurt his leg, it took some power away from him, especially his serve, and I was able to chase down more balls and be dangerous from the back of the court," Muster said.
The former French Open champion, once considered the world's best clay court player, improved to an impressive 21-3 on hard court this year.
"All players develop their techniques and their games and I'm at the point now where I'm probably better on hard courts than on clay," he said.
